title: Rooket's Wobbly Glow-Worms
markdown:
Nestled in the valley of Whisperwind, where the mountains tickled the clouds, life hummed along like a happy little brook. The ledges were lined with colourful stalls, and bouncy bridges hopped over deep green gorges. And every year, the most exciting event in all of Whisperwind was the annual Glow-Worm Garden Gala. This year, Goblin Rooket had a plan. A truly stupendous, top-secret plan!

Rooket was a goblin with fingers as nimble as dragonfly wings and a mind that fizzed with wonderfully peculiar ideas. He could coax the most marvellous things from the earth. This year, he’d spent weeks cultivating the brightest, most cheerful glow-worms you ever did clap eyes on. He’d arranged them in a pattern that looked like starlight sprinkled on moonbeams. Ah, but here's the thing about Rooket: he was terribly, terribly worried about appearing too eager. It wasn't proper, he felt, for a goblin to look like he was desperate for a win. "Oh dear," he'd muttered to himself, his pointy ears twitching like little antennae. "What if they see how much I want this? It’s dreadfully unbecoming." Worrying about what others think is a heavy load for such a clever little goblin. This thought, a tiny flutter of unease, was the first little wobble in his otherwise confident stride. It made his knees feel like wobbly jelly.

His best friend, Flint the ogre, was as different from Rooket as a mountain is from a pebble. Flint was enormous, his footsteps thundered like friendly drums, and his laughter was like a rumbling avalanche, but a very jolly one indeed. His heart, however, was softer than a dandelion puff in a gentle breeze. "Rooket, my friend!" Flint boomed, lumbering over. His voice was deep and warm, like a hug. "Ready for the Gala? I've polished my best acorn! See how it shines!" He held up a large, smooth acorn that glinted in the soft valley light.

Rooket waved a hand, trying very hard to look casual. "Ah, Flint. Just… observing. The potential for a garden of great delight is quite evident, wouldn't you agree? The air itself seems to be humming with excitement." And wouldn't you know it, Flint’s petunias were practically bursting with pride. "Oh, the most delight!" Flint nodded, a wide, gap-toothed grin spreading across his friendly face. "My petunias are practically… petal-ing with pride! They've never been so plump and pretty."

The day of the Gala arrived with a soft, sparkly drizzle that tap-tapped a cheerful rhythm against the mountain windows. Rooket, looking remarkably unruffled on the outside (though his left eyebrow was definitely doing a little jig of worry), surveyed his prize-winning glow-worm display. It was simply breathtaking. The tiny lights pulsed with a gentle, mesmerising glow, each one placed with perfect precision. Then, suddenly, with a ‘MAAAA!’ that sounded like a foghorn playing a trumpet, Barnaby the goat came galloping in! Barnaby had a peculiar knack for appearing when one least expected him, and usually when it was most inconvenient. He was a furry, bleating force of nature, with hooves that seemed to have a mind of their own.

Suddenly, with a cheerful "Maa!" that was far too loud and far too close, Barnaby trotted right through Rooket's carefully arranged glow-worms! The tiny lights scattered like startled fireflies. A few glow-worms, quite alarmed by the sudden commotion, zipped away into the shadowy crevices of the gorge. Rooket gasped, a tiny squeak of dismay escaping his lips. "Oh, Barnaby, you blundering beast! My starlight and moonbeams!"

And here's the curious thing about Barnaby: he was the only witness to the whole, calamitous event. He’d seen the entire, garden-ruining mishap. But Barnaby, bless his woolly heart, had the timing of a clock that had tumbled down a well and landed face-first. He just blinked, a tiny piece of stray glow-worm dust clinging to his beard like a sparkly speck of defiance.

Rooket’s knees felt like unset jelly. Panic, hot and sudden, flushed his neck. This was far worse than worrying about wanting to win. He felt a hot flush creep up his neck; his knees felt like unset jelly, threatening to buckle. This was not the sort of attention a goblin of refined taste wanted.

Flint, ever helpful and always ready to lend a hand (or an enormous foot), stomped over. "What's the matter, Rooket? Did a mischievous slug get into your prize petunias? Or perhaps a particularly grumpy ladybug?"

Rooket explained, his voice tight with worry. Flint looked from the scattered glow-worms to Barnaby, who was now nibbling contentedly on a particularly bright sprig of moss, completely unconcerned. "Right! We'll just… catch them!" Flint declared, and with that, he proceeded to chase Barnaby in wide, clumsy circles. He tripped over stray roots, narrowly missed toppling a precarious market stall selling fluffy cloud-cakes, and his booming laughter mixed with Barnaby's frantic bleating. It was less a capture, more a chaotic, rollicking dance, with dust stinging Rooket’s eyes and Flint’s laughter echoing off the mountainsides.

"No, no, Flint! Wait!" Rooket sighed, but even as he spoke, a tiny spark of an idea flickered to life in his clever mind. He looked at Barnaby, who was now doing a rather impressive jig, and then at the faint, twinkling trails where the glow-worms had gone. "You know, Flint," Rooket said, his voice suddenly calm and measured, a steely glint in his eye. "I believe I am not lost. I am simply taking the scenic route with great conviction." He winked at Flint, who stopped mid-stomp, looking utterly bewildered.

Rooket didn't chase. Instead, he very, very carefully began to coax the remaining glow-worms back into place. He used a large, iridescent beetle's wing, smooth as polished glass, to gently nudge them. He found a tiny dewdrop clinging to a leaf and used it to make the surrounding plants sparkle, just like tiny diamonds. He even found a few stragglers nestled near where Barnaby had been, looking quite content and even a little more luminous. And Barnaby, as if sensing Rooket’s calm purpose, seemed to naturally avoid the immediate area, content to munch on distant, less important foliage. He was like a fluffy white cloud drifting away from the main event.

When the judges, two very serious-looking sprites with wings like stained glass, finally arrived, Rooket’s garden was restored, perhaps even more magical than before. The glow-worms, having had a little adventure, seemed to shine with a newfound zest and vibrancy. Their light seemed to dance with pure joy.

The head sprite, whose wings shimmered with sapphire and emerald hues, peered at Rooket’s display. "Remarkable," she chirped, her voice like tiny silver bells. "Such… vibrant luminescence. And such a delightful, wild arrangement. It feels alive!"

Rooket, with a small, genuine smile that chased away any hint of worry, simply said, "Thank you. They do have a certain spirit, don't they? A little spark of their own."

And so it came to pass that Rooket won the Glow-Worm Garden Gala. He held the shimmering ribbon, a prize spun from moonlight, but as he watched the happy faces around him, a quiet warmth spread through his chest. A victory that felt as bright as the glow-worms themselves. It warmed him more than any ribbon ever could.

Later, as the last of the rain tapped a gentle, lullaby rhythm on the windowpanes, the village square glowed with the warm, friendly light of lanterns. The air smelled of roasted nuts, sweet berry cider, and something warm and comforting, like freshly baked bread. There was music, the gentle strumming of lutes, and the happy chatter of neighbours sharing stories. Rooket sat beside Flint, sharing a warm mug of honeyed milk. He watched the little lights of the village twinkling like fallen stars. No grand pronouncements, no boastful speeches. Just a cosy celebration, the soft murmur of contentment, and the warm glow of friendship. And that is the most enchanting prize of all.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
